adds.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part IV — The Niger State Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (Ostien, ed.)
adds.summary: Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

adds.title: Sharia Implementation in Northern Nigeria 1999-2006: A Sourcebook, Vol. IV, Ch. 4 Part III — The Sharia Penal Codes (Ostien, ed.)
adds.summary: The annotated sourcebook catalogue records Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, HB.4/2000, signed into law on 22 February 2000 and coming into operation on 4 May 2000 (Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8, 9 March 2000). The editor notes it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it merely amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. Confirms the state-specific enactment behind this record's claim that an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

adds.title: Suspected Gay Escapes Being Killed By Mob In Benin City – The Nigerian Observer
adds.summary: On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

adds.title: Police Declare Ugbogbo Ovbukhan Wanted Over Gay Practice – The Nigerian Observer
adds.summary: The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

adds.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.
